content: Epinephrine injection is prescribed to treat severe, life-threatening allergic reactions, also known as anaphylaxis. These reactions can be triggered by insect stings, certain foods, medications, latex, or other allergens. Symptoms of an allergic reaction may include wheezing, difficulty breathing, low blood pressure, hives, itching, swelling, stomach cramps, diarrhea, and loss of bladder control. Epinephrine belongs to a class of medications called sympathomimetic agents. It works by relaxing the muscles in the airways to improve breathing and constricting blood vessels to increase blood pressure. Epinephrine injection is available as a single-dose, pre-filled automatic injection device designed for administration into the thigh. It should only be used when you are experiencing or are likely to experience a severe allergic reaction. Discuss with your doctor the substances that may cause such reactions and the symptoms to watch for. In some cases, more than one dose of epinephrine may be required to manage the reaction. Your doctor will provide guidance on when and if a second dose is necessary. Always follow the instructions on your prescription label carefully, and consult your doctor or pharmacist if you have any questions. Use the epinephrine injection exactly as directed, and do not use more or less than prescribed. To use the automatic injection device, follow these steps: 1. Hold the device firmly in your fist with the black tip pointing downward. Avoid touching the black tip and hold only the cylinder. 2. Remove the gray activation cap. 3. Position the black tip near your outer thigh. 4. Swing your hand away from your body, then jab the black tip firmly into your outer thigh at a 90-degree angle. The needle can penetrate clothing if necessary. 5. Hold the device in place for several seconds. 6. Remove the device from your thigh and gently rub the injection site with your fingers. 7. Check the black tip to see if the needle is visible. If the needle is not visible, repeat steps 3–6. 8. If the needle is visible, the full dose of epinephrine has been delivered. Note that most of the liquid will remain in the device; this is extra liquid that cannot be used. 9. Press the needle against a hard surface, then place the device back into its carrying tube (without the activation cap) and cover it with the cap. After using the device: If the reaction was caused by an insect sting, try to remove the stinger with your fingernails. Avoid pushing the stinger deeper into the skin or pinching/squeezing the area. If possible, apply ice or a baking soda soak to the area. Go to the nearest hospital emergency room immediately and take the used injection device with you. Inform the doctor that you have used the device and give it to them for proper disposal. Rest and avoid physical activity as instructed by your doctor. Handle the automatic injection device carefully to prevent accidental injection into your hands or other areas. If accidental injection occurs, seek emergency medical attention immediately. Epinephrine injection may also be prescribed for other uses. Consult your doctor or pharmacist for more information. Before using epinephrine injection: Inform your doctor or pharmacist if you are allergic to epinephrine, sulfites, or any other medications. Your doctor may still recommend using epinephrine in life-threatening situations, even if you are allergic to one of its ingredients. The device does not contain latex and is safe for individuals with latex allergies. Provide your doctor or pharmacist with a list of all prescription and nonprescription medications, vitamins, nutritional supplements, and herbal products you are taking. Be sure to mention antidepressants (e.g., amitriptyline, clomipramine, nortriptyline), digoxin, quinidine, or monoamine oxidase inhibitors (e.g., phenelzine, tranylcypromine), especially if you have recently stopped taking them. Your doctor may need to adjust your medication doses or monitor you for side effects. Inform your doctor if you have a history of chest pain, heart attack, irregular heartbeat, diabetes, high blood pressure, or an overactive thyroid gland (hyperthyroidism). Let your doctor know if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. If you become pregnant while using epinephrine, contact your doctor. Unless otherwise directed by your doctor, continue your normal diet. Epinephrine injection may cause side effects. Notify your doctor if you experience any of the following minor side effects, especially if they persist or worsen: Upset stomach Vomiting Sweating Dizziness Nervousness Weakness Pale skin Headache Uncontrollable shaking of the hands Some side effects may be severe. Contact your doctor immediately if you experience: Difficulty breathing Pounding, fast, or irregular heartbeat Epinephrine injection may cause other side effects. Report any unusual problems to your doctor. Serious side effects can also be reported to the FDA’s MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program. Store the medication in its original plastic carrying tube, tightly closed, and out of reach of children. Keep it in a dark place at room temperature, away from excess heat and moisture (not in the bathroom). Regularly check the expiration date and ensure you always have an unexpired device available. Inspect the liquid in the device’s clear window periodically. Discard the device if the liquid has changed color, appears cloudy, contains solid particles, or if the expiration date has passed. Consult your pharmacist for proper disposal instructions. In an allergic emergency, if the liquid appears abnormal and no fresh device is available, consult your doctor for guidance. In case of overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the victim has collapsed or is not breathing, call 911 immediately. Keep all appointments with your doctor. Do not share your medication with others. Consult your pharmacist if you have questions about refilling your prescription. Brand names for epinephrine injection include: Adrenalin® Chloride Solution EpiPen® Auto-Injector EpiPen® Jr.
